all_historical_figures.name: Śiva
all_historical_figures.significance: Believed to be the divine originator of the Śaiva-Āgamas, revealing them to Pārvatī or other recipients.

all_historical_figures.name: Pārvatī
all_historical_figures.significance: Believed to be the recipient of wisdom from Śiva in Śaiva-Āgamas and the revealer of wisdom in Śākta-Āgamas.

all_historical_figures.name: Viṣṇu / Vāsudeva
all_historical_figures.significance: Believed to be the divine originator of the Vaiṣṇāva-Āgamas and a recipient of wisdom in some Śaiva-Āgamas.

all_historical_figures.name: Matanga
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as a recipient of the Matanga-Parameśvarāgama from Śiva.

all_historical_figures.name: Ruru
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as a recipient of the Rauravāgama from Śiva.

all_historical_figures.name: Śaṅkarṣaṇa
all_historical_figures.significance: In Vaiṣṇava tradition, the first 'vyūha' (emanation) from Vāsudeva, from whom the 'Āgama' originated.

all_historical_figures.name: Kātyāyana
all_historical_figures.significance: Cited for his definition of Tantra as 'the co-occurence of actions'.

all_historical_figures.name: Śabara
all_historical_figures.significance: Cited for his definition of Tantra, comparing it to a lamp that serves many students at once.

all_historical_figures.name: Kullūka-bhaṭṭa
all_historical_figures.significance: His gloss on Viṣṇu-purāṇa states that Veda and Tantra are the two main streams of Indian thought.

all_historical_figures.name: Indra, Varuṇa, Sūrya
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as examples of deified natural forces worshipped in the Brāhmaṇa texts for worldly gains.

all_historical_figures.name: Pāṇini
all_historical_figures.significance: His work, Aṣṭādhyāyī, mentions icons in households, indicating their existence prior to the Christian era.

all_historical_figures.name: Patañjali
all_historical_figures.significance: His work, Mahābhāṣya, also mentions household icons.

all_historical_figures.name: Kumārila
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of Tantra-vārtika; condemned Tāntric practices as non-Vedic.

all_historical_figures.name: Śaṅkara
all_historical_figures.significance: Mounted a severe attack on the non-Vedic approach of Tantra in his Vedānta-sūtra commentary.

all_historical_figures.name: Vallabha
all_historical_figures.significance: Attacked the Tāntric approach in his Anubhāṣya.

all_historical_figures.name: Appayya-dīkṣita
all_historical_figures.significance: Attacked the Tāntric approach in his commentary 'Parimala'.

all_historical_figures.name: Asparārka
all_historical_figures.significance: Commentator on Yājñavalkya-samhitā who argued against wholesale condemnation of Tantra, suggesting some parts are valid.

all_historical_figures.name: Abhinava-Gupta
all_historical_figures.significance: Extolled the Bhairava class of āgamas as the best.

all_historical_figures.name: Thāyumānavar
all_historical_figures.significance: Described the four stages corresponding to the pādas as bud, flower, raw fruit, and ripe fruit.

all_historical_figures.name: Manu
all_historical_figures.significance: Cited for the teaching that one must discharge worldly debts before seeking liberation.
all_historical_figures.dates: Ancient (text dated c. 2nd c. BCE - 2nd c. CE)

all_historical_figures.name: Patañjali
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as a literary source describing the practice of displaying icons for a living, which points to an early form of professional worship.
all_historical_figures.dates: 5th century B.C. (as stated in the text)

all_historical_figures.name: Mauryas
all_historical_figures.role: Mercenary priests (as described by Patañjali in the text)
all_historical_figures.significance: Cited as an early example of priests who earned a livelihood by performing worship for wealthy patrons.

all_historical_figures.name: Sadāśiva
all_historical_figures.significance: In Śaivāgama, he is considered the founder of the Āgama tradition and the ultimate source of the teaching lineage, which is passed down through human preceptors.

all_historical_figures.name: Heliodorus
all_historical_figures.significance: Erected a religious column in honour of Vāsudeva at Besnagar, providing one of the earliest inscriptional evidences of the Bhāgavata cult.

all_historical_figures.name: Gājāyana
all_historical_figures.significance: Constructed a stone-enclosure for the worship of Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva at Ghosuṇḍi.

all_historical_figures.name: Khāravela
all_historical_figures.significance: Recorded to have repaired temples of different sects, suggesting the existence of temples in the first century.

all_historical_figures.name: Hāla
all_historical_figures.significance: His work, Gāthā-saptaśatī, mentions the existence of temples.

all_historical_figures.name: Skanda-Mahāsena
all_historical_figures.significance: A temple dedicated to him is mentioned in the Bilsad inscription.

all_historical_figures.name: Kautilya
all_historical_figures.significance: His Artha-śāstra prescribes the building of temples for various deities, indicating state involvement in temple construction.

all_historical_figures.name: Appar, Sambandar and Sundara-mūrti
all_historical_figures.significance: Their compositions, known as 'tevāram' hymns, were taught in Śiva temples.

all_historical_figures.name: Āḻvārs
all_historical_figures.significance: Their compositions, known as 'prabhandam' hymnology, were taught in Vaiṣṇava shrines.

all_historical_figures.name: Varuṇa-śakti
all_historical_figures.significance: A renowned scholar who headed a major center of learning at the Kedāreśvara temple in Balligāme.

all_historical_figures.name: Keśava-deva
all_historical_figures.significance: Built a temple to Keśava in Balligāme and made provisions for thirty-eight scholars to reside there.

all_historical_figures.name: Śarvesvara-śakti-deva
all_historical_figures.significance: His maṭha is recorded to have had seventy-seven temples attached to it.

all_historical_figures.name: Tippu Sultan
all_historical_figures.significance: Initiated major changes in temple administration in 1788 by resuming temple lands and placing their management under state officials.

all_historical_figures.name: Kṛiṣṇarāja Odayar III
all_historical_figures.significance: Took personal interest in temple affairs and appointed local superintendents after the death of Tippu Sultan.

all_historical_figures.name: Sir Mark Cubbon
all_historical_figures.significance: As commissioner, he influenced the administration of temples in Mysore, at one point taking it out of the Commissioner's office.

all_historical_figures.name: Sir K. Sheshadri Iyer
all_historical_figures.significance: Found the administration of temples by Deputy Commissioners ineffective and appointed a separate Muzarai Superintendent.

complete_timeline.event: Inscription from Karnataka mentions volunteer administrators ('dharma-darsis')
complete_timeline.significance: Evidence for community involvement in temple administration.

complete_timeline.event: Inscription describing Varuṇa-śakti and the learning center at Balligāme
complete_timeline.significance: Provides evidence of temples functioning as universities.

complete_timeline.event: Tippu Sultan issues order resuming temple lands
complete_timeline.significance: Marks a significant shift towards state control over temple administration in Mysore.

complete_timeline.event: Death of Tippu Sultan and reorganization of administration by the British
complete_timeline.significance: Led to the inclusion of temple management (Muzarai) as a formal government responsibility.

complete_timeline.event: British Commissioner appoints 'pańcāyatdārs' to manage temples
complete_timeline.significance: An attempt to involve citizens in temple management under British rule.

complete_timeline.event: Commissioner takes over direct supervision of temples
complete_timeline.significance: Indicates the failure of the committee system and increased direct government control.
Brought all places of worship in Mysore under the sole charge of the Government.

complete_timeline.event: Mysore Religious and Charitable Institution Act (VII of 1927) passed
complete_timeline.significance: Solidified the Government as the chief controlling authority of temples in Mysore.

complete_timeline.date: Ancient (Pre-dates 2500 years before the text's writing)
complete_timeline.significance: Excavations at Mohenjodaro revealed icons (arcāmūrti), suggesting that the practice of icon worship in homes existed during this period.
Weakened the position of the distinct Āgama-tantra complex, especially practices considered extreme.

complete_timeline.event: Advent of iconoclast Muslims in North India
complete_timeline.significance: Created unrest and led to the custodians of Āgama literature fleeing to South India and Kaśmīr for refuge and patronage, causing a geographical shift in the tradition's development.
Led to the decline of the temple-oriented Śaiva-Āgama tradition in Kaśmīr, with only the philosophical portions surviving.

complete_timeline.date: Not earlier than the third or fourth century after Christ
complete_timeline.significance: Marks the period when public temples became a significant part of religious life, creating the context for the codification of Āgama literature.

complete_timeline.event: Śarvesvara-śakti-deva's maṭha recorded to have 77 temples
complete_timeline.significance: Shows the extensive association between monastic orders (maṭhas) and temples.

complete_timeline.event: Mention of a temple to Skanda-Mahāsena in the Bilsad inscription
complete_timeline.significance: Inscriptional evidence for temple existence in the Gupta period.

complete_timeline.event: Construction of a temple to Sūrya recorded in the Mandasor inscription
complete_timeline.significance: Inscriptional evidence for a temple with a high tower.

complete_timeline.event: Construction of earliest surviving structural temples (Bhitargāon, Deogarh)
complete_timeline.significance: Marks the beginning of monumental temple architecture in surviving evidence, credited to the Gupta dynasty.

complete_timeline.event: Construction of stone-enclosure at Ghosuṇḍi by Gājāyana
complete_timeline.significance: Early inscriptional evidence for a place of worship for Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva.

complete_timeline.event: Erection of Heliodorus' column at Besnagar
complete_timeline.significance: Earliest inscriptional evidence of a monument dedicated to Vāsudeva by a Bhāgavata enthusiast.

all_geographic_locations.context: Became a refuge for custodians of Āgama literature fleeing North India. The Siddhānta-āgama class found favorable conditions for consolidation here.
all_geographic_locations.significance: It is now the primary region where temple-context Śaiva-āgama is found and practiced.

all_geographic_locations.context: Served as a refuge for the Śaiva-Āgama tradition until the late 12th century. The Bhairava class of āgamas was prominent here.
all_geographic_locations.significance: After Muslim domination, the temple-orientation was lost, but the philosophical portions (Kashmir Śaivism) survived.

all_geographic_locations.context: The region where Āgama literature almost entirely disappeared due to Vedic opposition and Muslim invasions.
all_geographic_locations.significance: The historical heartland where the conflict between Āgama and Nigama traditions played out.

all_geographic_locations.context: Regions where some of the Āgama-tantra literature migrated.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Became centers for the preservation and development of Buddhist forms of Āgama/Tantra.

all_geographic_locations.context: Countries where the Buddhist variety of Āgama, focused on iconic worship (Sādhanā-texts), became prevalent.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Shows the wide geographical and cultural reach of Āgamic ideology.

all_geographic_locations.context: Associated with the Nātha-Siddha cult.
all_geographic_locations.significance: This area likely served as a conduit for the transmission of Āgamic ideas (primarily Śaiva and Śākta) into Jainism.

all_geographic_locations.context: The location where the practice of worshipping icons at home has existed for over 2500 years.
all_geographic_locations.significance: The cultural and geographical origin of the traditions being discussed.

all_geographic_locations.context: An archaeological site of the Indus Valley Civilisation.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Relics found here provide archaeological evidence for ancient icon worship in homes.

all_geographic_locations.context: Location where preceptors are known by specific titles.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Provides a geographical context for the living tradition and titles of Āgamic masters like Tantri, Āgamika, etc.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of the 2nd century B.C. Brāhmī inscription commemorating a religious column by Heliodorus.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Location of one of the earliest pieces of evidence for the Bhāgavata cult.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of a 1st century B.C. inscription recording the construction of a stone-enclosure for worship.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Early evidence for a shrine dedicated to Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva.

all_geographic_locations.context: Location of the earliest surviving structural brick temple, dated to the 5th century A.D.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A key archaeological site for early Hindu temple architecture.

all_geographic_locations.context: Location of the Daśāvatāra stone temple, also from the Gupta period (5th century A.D.).
all_geographic_locations.significance: An important early stone temple, though now in ruins.

all_geographic_locations.context: Home of the Jagannātha temple.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Example of a monumental temple with folk origins and continued mass appeal.

all_geographic_locations.context: Home of the Veṅkaṭeśvara temple.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Example of a monumental temple with folk origins and continued mass appeal.

all_geographic_locations.context: Home of the Mīnākṣi temple.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Example of a monumental temple with folk origins and continued mass appeal.

all_geographic_locations.context: Home of the Kāmākṣi temple.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Example of a monumental temple with folk origins and continued mass appeal.

all_geographic_locations.context: Home of the Kālī temple.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Example of a monumental temple with folk origins and continued mass appeal.

all_geographic_locations.context: Home of the Viśvanātha temple.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Example of a monumental temple with folk origins and continued mass appeal.

all_geographic_locations.context: Home of the Viṭhoba temple.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Example of a monumental temple with folk origins and continued mass appeal.

all_geographic_locations.context: Home of the Kṛiṣṇa temple.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Example of a monumental temple with folk origins and continued mass appeal.

all_geographic_locations.context: Home of the Mūkambika temple.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Example of a monumental temple with folk origins and continued mass appeal.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of the Kedāreśvara temple and the Koḍiya-maṭha.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A major center of learning (mahā-ghaṭikā-sthāna) in medieval South India.

all_geographic_locations.context: The erstwhile state used as a detailed case study for the evolution of temple administration.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Illustrates the transition from local/royal oversight to a structured government department (Muzarai).

complete_terminology_index.context: The central subject of the chapter; a body of texts and traditions dealing with worship, philosophy, and ritual.
Etymological root of Āgama, signifying knowledge that has 'come down' or been received.
One of the subjects Āgama provides knowledge about.
The opposite of dharma, which Āgama also clarifies.
The most ancient Hindu scriptures, also referred to as Nigama, often contrasted with the Āgamas.
One of the three main sectarian classifications of Āgamas.
One of the three main sectarian classifications of Āgamas.
One of the three main sectarian classifications of Āgamas.
The origin of language and the Āgamas, emanating from the absolute Śiva.
Describes the absolute state of Śiva from which creation and sound emanate.
The sacred sound that arose from the primordial nāda.
A major tradition of Vaiṣṇava Āgamas.
In Vaiṣṇava Āgama, the emanations of the absolute deity, Vāsudeva.
A term often used synonymously with Āgama, but more focused on technique and method.
A school of Hindu philosophy focused on Vedic exegesis, mentioned as a 'tantra' in the sense of an organized system.
Magical word-symbols used in Tāntric and Āgamic worship.
Designs used in Tāntric and Āgamic meditation and ritual.
The name typically given to the first chapter of Āgama texts.
Terms for the chief priest in a temple, used interchangeably.
Represented by the syllable 'ā' in an etymological breakdown of 'Āgama'.
Represented by the syllable 'ga' in an etymological breakdown of 'Āgama'.
Represented by the syllable 'ma' in an etymological breakdown of 'Āgama'.
A term used to stand for the Vedic tradition, in contrast to Āgama.
A primary requisite for salvation in the Āgamas.
The final step to emancipation in Āgamas; the primary focus in the Vedānta tradition.
An approach to the divine, made subordinate to devotion in the Āgamas.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Devotion is intense interest in worship and so on
complete_terminology_index.context: The Āgamic definition of devotion.
A figure of great importance in the Tāntric tradition, who bestows initiation.
A necessary and symbolic rite in the Tāntric tradition.
A body of secondary Hindu scriptures that advocated for deity worship, seen as a precursor to Āgama literature.
A genre of texts with popular appeal that had a complex, often antagonistic, relationship with the Āgamas.
Services to the deity that made worship more impressive in the Āgama tradition.
The four conventional books or sections of an Āgama text.
The first section of an Āgama, dealing with philosophy and theory.
The second section of an Āgama, dealing with spiritual practices for divine communion.
The third and most emphasized section of an Āgama, dealing with temple construction, rituals, and worship.
The fourth section of an Āgama, dealing with priestly conduct, observances, and festivals.
The acquisition of these powers is a topic in some Āgama texts, like those of the Vāma class.
The ultimate goal of spiritual endeavor, discussed in the Jñāna-pāda.
The highest degree of salvation, said to be the reward of the Vidyā-pāda.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Obtaining a form similar to the deity
complete_terminology_index.context: A level of salvation, the reward of the Yoga-pāda.
A level of salvation, the reward of the Kriyā-pāda.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Abiding in the same world as the deity
complete_terminology_index.context: The lowest level of salvation, the reward of the Caryā-pāda.
One of the two main goals of Āgamic practice, the distant objective.
One of the two main goals of Āgamic practice, the immediate objective.
Refers to worship performed by a priest for his own spiritual welfare, typically at home.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Worship for the sake of others
complete_terminology_index.context: Refers to the public worship performed by a priest in a temple on behalf of the community.
The body of scriptures primarily concerned with temple worship, rituals, and philosophy.
Refers to the physical icons found in Mohenjodaro excavations that were worshipped in homes.
Describes the interest of the priest who receives money for performing worship.
Describes both the interest of the patrons who receive blessings, and the fundamental purpose of temple worship.
Refers to worship carried out by a householder in their own home for personal benefit, primarily salvation.
A distinct, close-knit class of temple priests consecrated according to Āgamic rituals.
The specific ritual of consecration that qualifies a brahmin to become a temple priest, distinct from Vedic initiation.
Brahmins who are qualified only to worship at home and are not consecrated for temple worship.
Refers to brahmins who have undergone dīkṣā.
Another term for a consecrated brahmin qualified for temple worship in the Śaiva tradition.
How some texts (like Kāraṇāgama) describe worship for one's own sake (ātmārtha).
How some texts (like Kāraṇāgama) describe worship for the sake of others (parārtha).
The divine feminine consorts of gods, worshipped in temples to secure worldly benefits.
One of the three values of normal life sought through temple worship.
One of the three values of normal life sought through temple worship.
One of the three values of normal life sought through temple worship.
A variety of both home worship (of Śiva alone) and temple worship (ending with fire-oblation).
A variety of home worship.
A variety of home worship.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Worshipped by one with senses restrained
complete_terminology_index.context: A requirement for the 'pure' (śuddha) variety of home worship.
A learned master who can conduct worship; also a title for the head priest.
Describes home worship as being motivated by desires and spiritual benefits.
Describes the priest's attitude in temple worship; he does not seek personal spiritual benefits from his professional duties.
A variety of temple worship ending with a daily procession (nityotsavanta).
A variety of temple worship ending with a presentation of pure dance (śuddha-nṛttānta).
Describes the deity worshipped at home.
Describes the main deity installed in a temple.
The preceptor at whose hands the priest receives consecration.
Another term for the preceptor or master.
An unholy mix-up of different traditions, texts, or rituals, which is strongly forbidden.
Mixing different sectarian doctrines, like Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava.
Mixing different textual traditions within the same sect.
Mixing different conventional practices or rituals from different groups.
Changing preceptors or having multiple masters direct a single ritual sequence.
Refers to the ceremonial seed-sowing that begins major temple rituals.
The ritual of installing an icon in a temple.
Occasions of special worship in a temple requiring the preceptor's guidance.
A temple ritual requiring the preceptor's consultation.
The ritual of re-installing a damaged icon, guided by the preceptor.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Traditional doctrine or precept; a collection of scriptures.
complete_terminology_index.context: Refers to the vast body of literature that prescribes the rules for temple construction, worship, and rituals. The author identifies it as the major factor in the rise of temple culture.
Used to distinguish private, household worship from public worship in temples.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Local legends or histories of a place.
complete_terminology_index.context: Mentioned as sources that help trace the transformation of humble shrines into magnificent temples.
Mentioned in the Besnagar inscription, its presence suggests a shrine to Viṣṇu.
Mentioned in the Ghosuṇḍi inscription, suggesting a defined sacred space.
Refers to the cult whose emphasis on devotion (bhakti) encouraged the creation of public places of worship.
The devotional approach to Godhead that encouraged congregational worship.
A common designation for the mother-goddess, linking her worship to caves, which were precursors to the temple sanctum.
The iconic representation of a divinity.
The aniconic representation of Śiva.
The technical term for the consecrated image in a temple or home that is the focus of worship.
The temple is metaphorically described as the 'body' of the godhead.
The image in the sanctum is described as the 'soul' of the temple.
A classification of temples where the image is a self-manifestation of Godhead.
A classification for temples built by human beings in recent times.
Classifications of temples based on the number of building materials used (one, two, or three respectively).
The term for the six-part vertical division of a South Indian temple.
The lowest part of the temple's vertical structure.
The superstructure over the sanctum.
A term for the superstructure, sometimes used for the entire sanctum structure.
The sanctum sanctorum of the temple, housing the main deity.
Roofed halls, either attached or detached from the main shrine, used for various functions (assembly, dance, marriage, etc.).
The surrounding wall of a temple complex.
The monumental, towered gateway in the prākāra of a temple.
Food that has first been offered to the deity (naivedya) and is then distributed to devotees.

complete_terminology_index.translation: Place of a great educational institution; university.
complete_terminology_index.context: Refers to temples that functioned as major centers of learning.
Monastic organizations that were often associated with temples.
The annual temple festival, which is a major social and economic event.
The administrative council of a temple, consisting of local dignitaries.
The hereditary administrator or manager of a temple.
The official name for the government department in Mysore responsible for managing temple and charitable endowments.
Describes public worship performed by a priest for the benefit of the community, as opposed to private worship (ātmārtha).
The chief priest who performs worship in the sanctum sanctorum.
